name: Alcohol
shortDesc: A depressant that affects the central nervous system.

myths.myth: Alcohol is not a drug because it's legal.
myths.fact: Alcohol is a psychoactive drug. Legal status doesn't determine whether something is a drug.
Coffee only makes you more alert while still intoxicated. It doesn't reduce blood alcohol level.

regionalContext: Traditional beer (doro) is deeply embedded in Shona and Ndebele culture. Understanding the line between cultural practice and harmful use is essential.

name: Tobacco
shortDesc: A highly addictive plant product containing nicotine.

myths.fact: Light cigarettes still cause cancer and heart disease. There is no safe cigarette.
Hookah smoking carries many of the same health risks as cigarette smoking.

regionalContext: Tobacco is Zimbabwe's largest export crop, but local consumption rates are rising, especially among youth.

name: Cannabis (Marijuana)
shortDesc: A psychoactive plant that affects memory, mood, and coordination.

myths.fact: About 9% of users develop dependence. This rises to 17% for those who start in adolescence.
Regular use can affect brain development in teens and lead to respiratory issues.

regionalContext: Known locally as 'mbanje', cannabis use is widespread but carries legal penalties. Medicinal use is being explored globally.

name: Methamphetamine
shortDesc: A highly addictive synthetic stimulant that damages the brain.

myths.fact: Methamphetamine is one of the most addictive substances known. Most users cannot control their use.

myths.myth: Crystal meth is different from meth.
myths.fact: Crystal meth is simply a crystalline form of methamphetamine. Same drug, same dangers.

regionalContext: Known as 'mutoriro' or 'guka', meth use has surged in Zimbabwe's urban areas, particularly among young people.

name: Prescription Drug Misuse
shortDesc: Using prescription medications in ways other than directed.

myths.myth: Prescription drugs are safe because a doctor prescribed them.
myths.fact: When misused, prescription drugs can be just as dangerous as illegal substances.

myths.myth: Taking more than prescribed works faster.
myths.fact: Overdosing on prescription drugs can cause organ failure and death.

regionalContext: Access to prescription medications without proper oversight is common. Codeine-based cough syrups are frequently misused.

name: Peer Pressure
shortDesc: Social pressure to conform to group behaviour.
content: Peer pressure is one of the strongest factors in teen substance initiation. Learning to recognise and resist it is a critical life skill.
regionalContext: In Zimbabwe, peer pressure often intersects with 'ubuntu' values of community. Finding culturally appropriate ways to assert individual choice is key.

name: Refusal Skills
content: Being able to say no confidently is one of the most protective skills against substance abuse. Practice makes it easier.
regionalContext: Role-playing scenarios that reflect local situations (e.g., graduation parties, sports events) makes practice more relevant.

name: Mental Health
shortDesc: Understanding mental health and when to seek help.
content: Mental health conditions often co-occur with substance use. Addressing both is essential for recovery.
regionalContext: Mental health stigma is significant in Zimbabwe. The Friendship Bench project offers a culturally appropriate model for community-based mental health support.

name: Healthy Coping Strategies
shortDesc: Positive ways to manage stress and emotions.
content: When stress feels overwhelming, healthy coping strategies provide alternatives to substance use. Find what works for you.
regionalContext: Traditional practices like community gathering, storytelling (ngano), and music can be powerful coping tools.

name: The Science of Addiction
shortDesc: How substances hijack the brain's reward system.
content: Addiction is a brain disease, not a moral failing. Substances flood the brain with dopamine, creating artificial highs that the brain becomes dependent on.
regionalContext: Understanding addiction as a medical condition helps reduce stigma in communities where substance use is often seen as 'lack of willpower'.
